title: The Bavan Akhri's heart
hook: cleverness without the Name goes nowhere, says one letter of the Bavan Akhri (Gauri, ang 260)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan's fifty-two letters: an acrostic where each letter opens a lesson, and the Guru is mother and father. Your line was the letters again. What lesson did the first letter of your name carry? Day one thousand two hundred one.

Can a person know a great deal and still miss the point? Maybe you've met one: the uncle who can win any argument at the table and somehow never seems happy, the friend who's read everything about love and can't keep a friendship going. Knowing isn't the problem. Something is missing from the middle of it. The Bavan Akhri hands that lesson to one letter of the alphabet. Today, the heart of the fifty-two letters.
screen: `KNOWING A GREAT DEAL.` → `STILL MISSING THE POINT.` → `ONE LETTER'S LESSON.`

segments.voice: The letter is sassa, the S sound in Gurmukhi. Here is its stanza, paraphrased. Sassa: give up your cleverness, you who don't understand. The Lord is not won over by clever tricks or by giving orders. You may try a thousand kinds of cleverness, but not one of them will go with you. Hear the play on the letter: sassa opens with siaanap, cleverness. The alphabet itself is teaching. A few days back, Guru Amar Das told the restless mind that no one finds the Lord through cleverness. Guru Arjan's stanza takes a different turn: it asks what your cleverness can carry with you. Now turn it a few ways. First, what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't say learning is bad. This is a hymn built out of the alphabet itself. Guru Arjan isn't against letters. He's against a certain use of them. Second, the two things named: clever tricks and commands. Being smart enough to get your way, and powerful enough to order it. Both are ways of staying in control. The stanza says the Lord isn't won by either. Third, the thousand kinds. You can multiply your cleverness as far as you like, and not one of them goes with you. That's the stanza's measure: not how much you know, but what goes with you. And in Sikh teaching, what goes with you is the Name. So that's the Bavan Akhri's heart. Learning is welcome. Letters are a gift. But learning without the Name at its center is like a beautifully built house with nobody living in it. What the Guru asks of his students isn't less knowledge. It's knowledge with a heart: learned humbly, held loosely, and pointed toward the Name.
screen: `SASSA: GIVE UP YOUR CLEVERNESS.` · `NOT AGAINST LETTERS, AGAINST A USE.` · `A THOUSAND KINDS, NONE GOES WITH YOU.` · `KNOWLEDGE WITH THE NAME AT ITS CENTER.` · then, large: `THE BAVAN AKHRI'S HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing for its heart. In the sit, bring to mind something you're learning right now: a skill for work, a language, a recipe, a hymn. Then ask it one quiet question: what are you for? Not what will you get me, but who or what could you serve? Let an answer come, even a small one. Hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Bavan Akhri's heart. Sassa's lesson: give up your cleverness; a thousand kinds of it won't go with you, but the Name will. Today's word.
Your line: learning with heart. The next time you learn something today, even something small, ask it the sit's question: what are you for? Day one thousand two hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers turn to stanzas like this one when they speak of learning held with humility and pointed toward the Name.

notes: The sassa stanza 'sasa siaanap chhaad iaana, hikmat hukam na prabh patiaana, sahas bhaat karah chaturaai, sang tuhaarai ek na jaai' is placed in Gauri Bavan Akhri M5, Ang 260, from memory; please confirm the Ang and paraphrase.

The outline hook says 'learning without the Name is empty'; the script draws that from the sassa stanza and frames the conclusion as Sikh teaching. Please confirm a Keeper is comfortable with this reading.
